Early learning

A kindergarten-readiness checklist for Sri Lankan families.

Readiness is not a race to read first or finish the most worksheets. It is the growing ability to join a group, communicate a need, try a task and recover when something feels unfamiliar.

By Princeway CollegePublished 6 November 20267 minute read

Families often ask what a child should know before kindergarten. The most useful answer begins with what a child can do for themselves and with others—not how many pages they can complete.

A child does not need to arrive at school fully independent, fluent in English or already reading. Kindergarten exists to develop these capacities. Preparation should make the new environment easier to enter, not turn the months before school into an examination.

Everyday independence

Small self-care skills give children a sense of control during a busy school day. Practise them slowly at home, allowing enough time for the child to attempt the task before an adult steps in.

  • Open and close a lunch box and water bottle.
  • Carry and recognise their own bag and belongings.
  • Use the toilet with age-appropriate independence and ask for help when needed.
  • Wash and dry hands.
  • Put on or remove simple clothing and footwear.
  • Tidy one activity before starting another.

Label belongings clearly, but also teach the child what their name looks like. A familiar symbol beside the name can help younger children identify items without anxiety.

Communication before perfect language

A kindergarten child needs ways to express basic needs: “I need help,” “I don’t understand,” “May I have water?” or “I feel unwell.” These sentences can be practised in the language used at school, but the goal is confident communication rather than perfect pronunciation.

At home, give the child time to finish a thought. Ask open questions about pictures, play and daily events. When adults answer too quickly on a child’s behalf, the child loses a safe opportunity to organise words and make themselves understood.

Joining a group

School involves waiting, listening, sharing materials and moving from one activity to another. These skills develop through practice. Board games, family meals, group play and simple household tasks all teach turn-taking and cooperation.

Children will still interrupt, become impatient or struggle to share. Readiness does not mean these behaviours disappear. It means the child is beginning to understand the routine and can respond to calm adult guidance.

A ready child is not a child who never needs help. It is a child who is gradually learning how to seek help, accept guidance and try again.

Early literacy without pressure

Reading aloud is one of the most useful preparations for school. Choose short stories, poems, picture books and familiar tales. Talk about the cover, predict what may happen and let the child retell the story in their own words.

Notice letters in meaningful places: the child’s name, a shop sign, a bus destination or a food label. Sing songs with rhyme and rhythm. Draw, colour, tear paper, build with blocks and use dough; these activities strengthen the hand control that later supports writing.

Correcting every mistake can make early literacy feel risky. Instead, respond to the idea first. If a child tells an imaginative story from a picture, that language work matters even when no printed words are being read.

Numbers through ordinary life

Count steps, fruit, spoons or toy cars. Compare which container holds more, sort laundry by colour and notice simple shapes around the home. These experiences give numbers meaning before children meet formal written tasks.

Play also develops planning, memory and flexible thinking. A child building a road from blocks is making decisions about length, balance and space. An adult can extend the learning with a question—“What could make this stronger?”—without taking over the activity.

Prepare the body and the routine

In the weeks before school, move gradually towards the expected waking, meal and bedtime routine. Practise eating the kind of snack or lunch the child will carry. If the journey is new, make it together and describe what will happen from leaving home to being collected.

Avoid promising that the child will never feel worried or that every day will be fun. A more trustworthy message is: “New things can feel strange. Your teachers will help you, and I will come back after school.”

Plan for the first weeks

Children often hold themselves together at school and release strong feelings at home. Tiredness, clinginess or irritability can appear even when the day went well. Keep afternoons simple where possible, offer food and rest, and ask gentle questions rather than requesting a full report immediately.

A five-minute evening check

  • What made you smile today?
  • Was anything difficult?
  • Who did you spend time with?
  • Is there something you want your teacher or family to help with tomorrow?

If a concern continues, share specific observations with the teacher. “She has cried before school for five days and says she cannot find the toilet” is more useful than “She hates school.” Clear information helps home and school solve the right problem together.

Children develop at different rates. This checklist is a general family guide, not a developmental assessment. Discuss persistent concerns with your child’s teacher and an appropriately qualified professional.
